Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

We represent: appellant defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a traffic stop becomes unlawful when officers extend it beyond the time reasonably needed without reasonable suspicion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Tenth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. The Officers Unlawfully Extended the Traffic Stop Beyond the Time Reasonably Required, Without Reasonable Suspicion of Other Criminal Activity.

**A. A traffic stop may last only as long as needed to complete its mission.**

A traffic stop is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment and is analyzed under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1 (1968). *United States v. Botero-Ospina*, 71 F.3d 783, 786–87 (10th Cir. 1995) (en banc). The inquiry has two parts: whether the stop was justified at its inception, and whether the resulting detention was reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified it. *Id.* The Supreme Court has made clear that "a police stop exceeding the time needed to handle the matter for which the stop was made violates the Constitution's shield against unreasonable seizures." *Rodriguez v. United States*, 575 U.S. 348, 350 (2015). Authority for the seizure "ends when tasks tied to the traffic infraction are—or reasonably should have been—completed." *Id.* at 354.

The tasks tied to the infraction are limited: checking the driver's license, registration, and insurance, running warrants checks, and issuing a citation. *Id.* at 354–55. This Court has long applied the same limits. *See United States v. Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d 1345, 1349 (10th Cir. 1998); *United States v. Mendez*, 118 F.3d 1426, 1429–31 (10th Cir. 1997). Once those tasks are done, or reasonably should have been done, the officer must allow the driver to proceed unless the driver consents to further questioning or the officer has an objectively reasonable and articulable suspicion of other criminal activity. *United States v. Bradford*, 423 F.3d 1149, 1156–57 (10th Cir. 2005); *United States v. West*, 219 F.3d 1171, 1176 (10th Cir. 2000). Unrelated inquiries and investigative detours, including a dog sniff, may not lengthen the stop absent that suspicion. *Rodriguez*, 575 U.S. at 355–57.

**B. The officers prolonged the stop after its mission was, or should have been, complete.**

[Insert record-specific facts: time of stop; time the license, registration, and warrants checks returned clean; time the officer began or completed the citation; the point at which Appellant was held for additional questioning or a canine sniff. *See* Aplt. App. __.] By that point the tasks tied to the traffic violation were complete, or reasonably should have been. Everything that followed was an independent investigation, unrelated to the stop's mission, that added time to the detention. Under *Rodriguez*, that extension was lawful only if supported by consent or reasonable suspicion. 575 U.S. at 357.

**C. The officers lacked reasonable suspicion to justify the extension.**

Reasonable suspicion requires "a particularized and objective basis" for suspecting criminal activity, and it demands more than an inchoate hunch. *United States v. Karam*, 496 F.3d 1157, 1161–62 (10th Cir. 2007). The government bears the burden of showing it existed. This Court has repeatedly rejected the kinds of factors typically offered to justify prolonged roadside detentions. Nervousness during a police encounter is of limited significance because it is common among innocent people. *West*, 219 F.3d at 1178–79; *United States v. Edgerton*, 438 F.3d 1043, 1048–51 (10th Cir. 2006). Travel plans that are merely unusual, or a driver's use of a rental or third-party vehicle, do not supply reasonable suspicion either. *United States v. Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d 892, 896–900 (10th Cir. 2004); *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350–51. Nor does a collection of innocent factors become suspicious simply because it is listed together. *Edgerton*, 438 F.3d at 1051; *West*, 219 F.3d at 1179.

The factors the government relied on here ([list, e.g., nervousness, travel itinerary, odor of air freshener, criminal history]) are of exactly this kind. Even taken together, they describe the behavior of many lawful travelers and do not give rise to a particularized suspicion of drug trafficking or any other crime. [Tailor to record.] Appellant did not consent to the continued detention, and mere acquiescence to an officer's show of authority is not consent. *See Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350.

**D. Suppression is required.**

Because the detention became unlawful once the stop's mission was, or should have been, complete, everything obtained through the extended detention, including [the canine alert, the search of the vehicle, and Appellant's statements], is fruit of the unlawful seizure and must be suppressed. *Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 484–88 (1963). The district court's contrary ruling should be reversed.
